title: Cloud & Deployment Fundamentals for Go — Revision

sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Cloud deployment questions at the fresher level test whether you understand the operational context your code runs in. Go's fast startup, small binary, and low memory footprint make it well-suited for containerised cloud environments, and interviewers at cloud-native companies ask about this directly. Knowing how to add a health check endpoint, read config from environment variables, and emit structured logs are table-stakes for joining any team running Go services in production.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body:
Three properties of Go that drive cloud deployment decisions:

- **Fast startup enables Kubernetes autoscaling.** A Go service starts in under 100 ms. A JVM service takes 1-3 seconds. For Kubernetes horizontal pod autoscaling, cold-start time determines how quickly you can respond to traffic spikes.
- **Configuration belongs in environment variables, not config files.** This is the twelve-factor app principle: separate config from code. `os.Getenv("DATABASE_URL")` reads config at runtime without rebuilding the binary. Different environments (dev/staging/prod) just set different env vars.
- **Structured logs (JSON) make log aggregation work.** `log.Printf("user logged in: %s", userID)` is hard to query in Datadog, Splunk, or CloudWatch. `slog.Info("user logged in", "user_id", userID)` emits `{"level":"INFO","msg":"user logged in","user_id":"123"}` — fields are queryable.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
- **Go binary deployment** — single static binary, no runtime dependencies; `go build -o server ./cmd/server`; copy binary to server or container and run it
- **Twelve-factor app for Go** — config via env vars (not config files); logs to stdout (not files); stateless processes (no local state that cannot be lost); these three factors are what interviewers test
- **Health check endpoint** — `http.HandleFunc("/healthz", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) { w.WriteHeader(200) })` — Kubernetes liveness and readiness probes hit this endpoint; a 200 response means the pod is healthy
- **Kubernetes basics for Go** — a `Deployment` YAML with `image`, `ports`, `readinessProbe` pointing to `/healthz`, `resources.requests` and `resources.limits` for CPU and memory
- **Environment config in Go** — `os.Getenv("DATABASE_URL")` for simple reads; `os.LookupEnv("PORT")` returns `(value, ok)` to distinguish unset from empty; struct-based config with the `envconfig` library for larger services
- **Logging basics** — `log.Printf` writes to stderr; `log/slog` (Go 1.21+) for structured JSON logs: `slog.Info("request", "path", r.URL.Path, "status", 200)` — prefer slog in new code

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- **Liveness vs readiness probe** — liveness: 'is the process alive?' (restart if fails); readiness: 'is it ready to serve traffic?' (remove from load balancer if fails). A Go service should expose both, typically at `/healthz` (liveness) and `/readyz` (readiness). Readiness can check database connectivity; liveness should be lightweight.
- **Go containers cold-start in milliseconds** — compared to JVM services (1-3 seconds to load classes). For serverless/FaaS or K8s autoscaling, this is the key advantage. Interviewers ask: 'why choose Go over Java for a serverless function?'
- **Never log secrets** — `slog.Info("config", "db_url", dbURL)` may log the database password. Always redact sensitive fields. The structured logging pattern makes it easier to audit what is being logged.
- **`os.Getenv` returns empty string, not an error** — unlike `os.LookupEnv`, `os.Getenv` cannot tell you if a variable is unset vs set to empty. For required config, use `os.LookupEnv` and fail fast at startup if the variable is missing.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: > *"A Go service is easy to deploy in the cloud because it compiles to a single static binary with no runtime dependencies and starts in under 100 milliseconds. I follow twelve-factor principles: config comes from environment variables read with `os.Getenv`, logs go to stdout as structured JSON using `log/slog`. I always add a `/healthz` endpoint for Kubernetes readiness and liveness probes — it returns 200 when the service is healthy and is the first thing a Kubernetes operator checks when a pod is not receiving traffic."*
